passage:
Dolma stood in the kitchen doorway. "Amala, everyone's going to Simran's birthday dinner. It ends at nine. Why can't I?"
"Because you'd be coming back alone after dark. The answer is no, Dolma."
Dolma's jaw set. She went to her room and didn't slam the door, but she didn't come out for dinner either. Lying on the bed, she felt like a little kid again.
An hour later she came back.
"Amala, can I say something without fighting?"
"Try."
"When you say no to everything after dark, I miss things that matter to me. Simran's my best friend. It feels like you think I'm still a child."
"I don't think that. I think the road is dark."
"What if Simran's father drops me to our gate, and I call you when I leave and when I'm in the car? One try. If anything goes wrong, you can say no next time."
Amala dried her hands slowly. "Call me when you leave. Not a text. A call."
"Deal."

qa.q: What time does Simran's birthday dinner end?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel lying on her bed?
qa.a: Resentful and small, as if she were being treated like a little kid.

qa.q: What made Dolma's second attempt work better than staying in her room?
qa.a: She calmly explained what the rule cost her and offered a one-time trial with a lift and a call.

qa.q: What was behind Amala's no?
qa.a: Worry about Dolma coming home alone on a dark road, not a belief that Dolma is a child.

grounding: A teenager stewing in resentment over a parent's restriction calmly says what the rule costs her and offers a trial of trust instead of sulking.

passage:
I'm Pema. The year I turned fifteen, my parents banned me from the evening cricket nets because the ground was across the highway. I felt as if they saw me as a baby. For a week I barely spoke at home. I slammed my door, and I stopped doing my homework properly, as if bad marks would punish them. My brother Vijay said, "You're only hurting yourself." I hated that he was right.
One Sunday I sat down with Papa. I told him the nets were the only place I felt good at something, and the ban was costing me my place on the team. Then I offered a plan: Vijay would come with me for a month, and I'd call when we crossed the highway. Papa agreed to a trial.
It worked. Looking back, the week of slammed doors got me nothing. One calm talk got me the nets.

qa.q: Why were Pema's parents worried about the evening nets?
qa.a: The ground was across the highway.

qa.q: How did Pema feel during the week of silence?
qa.a: Resentful and babied, and annoyed that Vijay was right.

qa.q: What was wise in Pema's talk with Papa, and what had been immature before?
qa.a: Calmly explaining what the ban cost and offering a trial was wise; slamming doors and neglecting homework to punish them was immature.

qa.q: How did Vijay see Pema's slammed doors and poor homework?
qa.a: As self-defeating; Vijay said it was only hurting Pema.

grounding: A teenager resentful of a parental ban first sulks and lets studies slip, then calmly states the cost and proposes a trial of trust.

passage:
Pankaj's father had said no again. "The highway to Jalgaon is dangerous. Take the bus."
"The bus takes three hours, Baba! You don't even know how anything works now," Pankaj snapped. Then, under his breath, to his cousin Pranav: "Village thinking. They still believe the radio is the internet."
Pranav, who had just got his licence, didn't laugh. "Your Baba lost his friend Suresh on that highway, remember? He's not stupid. He's scared."
Pankaj went quiet. He had forgotten Suresh Kaka.
That evening he sat beside Baba on the charpai. "Baba, I spoke rudely. I still think the bus is too slow. What if I go pillion with Pranav, both of us in helmets, and never after dark?"
Baba looked out at the dark field for a long time. "Show me the helmets first."

qa.q: Which friend of Baba's died on the highway?
qa.a: Suresh Kaka.

qa.q: What was behind Pankaj's "village thinking" remark?
qa.a: Frustration turning into contempt; he was seeing Baba as clueless so his words stopped counting.

qa.q: How did Pankaj move from sneering to a wiser approach?
qa.a: He apologised for being rude and proposed a safer plan that answered Baba's actual fear.

qa.q: How does Baba likely see the highway?
qa.a: As a real danger, because he lost his friend Suresh on it.

grounding: A teenager begins to sneer at his father as backward, then separates the father's fear from his old-fashioned ways and hears the concern.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Friday
Swati came in with her mother, Mrs. Alka Desai, after weeks of arguments about outings. Swati said, "Every time I ask to go anywhere, she says no. It's like I'm a walking disaster." Her mother's hands were twisting in her lap.
I asked Swati to try one question: "What exactly are you afraid of, Mumma?" There was a long silence. Then her mother listed them: the autos at night, the older boys at the cafe, and what the neighbours say. Swati looked surprised. "You never said any of that."
We took them one by one. Autos: Swati shares her live location. The cafe: on weekdays she meets friends at the library instead. The neighbours: her mother admitted that one was hers to handle. They left planning one Saturday outing as a trial.

qa.q: Where will Swati meet friends on weekdays?
qa.a: At the library instead of the cafe.

qa.q: How did Swati feel before the session?
qa.a: Frustrated and resentful, as if she were treated like a walking disaster.

qa.q: What question helped, and why?
qa.a: "What exactly are you afraid of, Mumma?" It turned a vague fear into specific worries that could be handled one by one.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Desai's twisting hands and her list reveal?
qa.a: That her rules came from love mixed with anxiety about night autos, older boys and gossip.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager learning that her parent's restrictions come from love and anxiety, and asking exactly what is feared so it can be addressed.

passage:
Saturday
Mom said no to the Diwali night cycle ride with Eshaan's group AGAIN. I nearly exploded. Then I noticed her face. She wasn't angry. She looked scared. She kept glancing at the TV news about the flyover accident.
So instead of shouting, I asked, "What exactly are you worried about?" She took a breath and said three things: the traffic after dark, the older boys in Eshaan's building who smoke, and me not picking up my phone.
Honestly? Two of those are fair. So I offered: we ride only on the colony roads, I carry a charged phone and answer every call, and I skip the older boys' group. She said yes, for tonight, and hugged me for too long.
Weird, being the thing my mom is scared for. But I kind of get it now.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Which news was Mom glancing at?
qa.a: The TV news about the flyover accident.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on noticing Mom's face?
qa.a: Surprised to see she was scared, not angry, and the urge to explode cooled.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav address Mom's specific fears?
qa.a: By offering to ride only on colony roads, carry a charged phone and answer every call, and skip the older boys' group.

qa.q: How might Mom have felt when she hugged Vaibhav for too long?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful that her fears were heard and turned into a plan.

grounding: A teenager notices a parent's restriction comes from love and anxiety, asks exactly what is feared and addresses it.

passage:
Seema stood at the door of the study. "Papa, I'll be home by seven like you said. But I want you to know I think it's too early."
Papa looked up from the newspaper. "You'll follow it, though?"
"Yes. You've been fair with me before, so I'll trust you on this one. But it means I miss the combined study group at Kamal's house, and that group really helps me with physics."
"Kamal's house is across the flyover..."
"I know. I'm not asking to break the rule. I'm asking to talk about it again after the exams."
Papa folded the paper. "That's a fair way to put it."
"And Papa? I'm not going to pretend I'm happy about it."
He laughed. "Good. I'd worry if you did."

qa.q: By what time must Seema be home?
qa.a: By seven.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about the rule?
qa.a: Unhappy and in disagreement, but trusting Papa because he has been fair before.

qa.q: Why is Seema's approach wiser than just swallowing her wish?
qa.a: She follows the rule but says her disagreement openly and asks to negotiate again after the exams.

qa.q: How does Papa see Seema's honesty?
qa.a: He appreciates it as fair, and would worry if she pretended to be happy.

grounding: A teenager follows a disliked rule because her parent has earned trust, while openly stating her disagreement and asking to negotiate later.

passage:
I'm Rashmi. When I was fifteen, my parents made a rule: phones on the dining table by ten every night. I hated it. My friends' group chat came alive at exactly ten.
The first month, I said nothing and just obeyed, smiling. Inside I was boiling. My brother Pranav said I looked like a pressure cooker about to whistle. He was right. Swallowing it made everything worse.
So I changed how I did it. I kept following the rule, because my parents had never set a rule just to control me. But at dinner I said clearly, "I think ten is too early on weekends, and I'm missing things." We argued, politely. They agreed to eleven on Saturdays.
Looking back, what mattered wasn't winning the extra hour. It was learning that I could obey and still say what I thought.

qa.q: What time did Rashmi's parents agree to on Saturdays?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How was Rashmi feeling during the first month of silent obeying?
qa.a: Boiling inside, resentful while smiling on the outside.

qa.q: What did Rashmi learn to do instead of swallowing the wish?
qa.a: Keep following the rule but state the disagreement clearly and negotiate, which won eleven on Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Pranav see Rashmi during that first month?
qa.a: Like a pressure cooker about to whistle; Pranav noticed the hidden anger.

grounding: A teenager who first swallows a disliked rule learns to follow it out of earned trust while openly disagreeing and negotiating.

passage:
Thursday night
Mum said yes to the concert. I should be happy. I'm not.
Because I know how I got it. I went quiet at dinner, let my eyes fill up, said, "It's fine, I never get to do anything anyway." Mum gave in within five minutes. It works almost every time.
Afterwards Francis texted, "let me guess, the sad-face thing again?" I laughed, but it stung. It's become a habit. I don't even plan it now. And it leaves me feeling slippery, like I can't trust my own tears.
So tomorrow I'm going to tell Mum the truth: that I really want to go, who's going, how I'll get home, and that I'll call at eleven. If she still says yes, it'll be a real yes. If she says no, at least it's honest.
Vidya

qa.q: At what time does Vidya plan to call?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: Why isn't Vidya happy about the yes?
qa.a: Vidya feels slippery and uneasy, knowing the yes came from a guilt-trip habit, not honesty.

qa.q: What honest case does Vidya plan to make?
qa.a: Telling Mum how much the concert matters, who is going, how the trip home will work, and promising a call at eleven.

qa.q: How might Mum feel if she learned how the yes was won?
qa.a: Probably hurt and less trusting, since she gave in to what she thought were real tears.

grounding: A teenager notices a habit of using tears and guilt to get a yes, feels slippery, and decides to make an honest case instead.

passage:
I'm Eshaan. The year I turned fifteen, I changed fast. New friends, like Sahil from the skating group, earphones in all the time, one-word answers at dinner. And Mom clamped down. Suddenly there was a curfew, questions about every message, and my door had to stay open.
I thought she was being a jailer. Then one night I heard her on the phone with Masi: "He's become a stranger in my own house. I feel shut out." Her voice cracked.
That hit me. I had been shutting her out and calling her controlling for noticing.
So I tried something. Every morning I told her my plan for the day: where, with whom, when back. I brought Sahil home to meet her. It felt silly at first. But within a month the open-door rule vanished, and the curfew moved an hour later. Sharing freely got me more freedom than fighting ever did.

qa.q: Who was Eshaan's new friend from the skating group?
qa.a: Sahil.

qa.q: How did Mom feel when Eshaan changed?
qa.a: Shut out and hurt; she said he had become a stranger in her own house, and her voice cracked.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do that lowered Mom's need to control?
qa.a: He told her his plans each day, where, with whom and when back, and brought Sahil home to meet her.

qa.q: How did Eshaan's view of Mom change after the phone call?
qa.a: He stopped seeing her as a jailer and saw a worried mother who felt shut out.

grounding: A teenager whose mother clamps down after he changes learns she feels shut out, and by sharing plans freely lowers her need to control and gains freedom.

passage:
Counsellor's note, family session
Mrs. Kalyani Iyer asked for this meeting. Since Uma stopped dance class and began spending evenings in her room, her mother has been taking her phone at nine, checking her bag and banning sleepovers. "I don't know my daughter any more," she said, and then, quietly, "I feel locked outside her life."
Uma rolled her eyes, then saw her mother's face and stopped. She said she quit dance because she was tired of it, not because of anything bad, and that her evenings were mostly music and one friend.
I suggested a small experiment: Uma tells her mother her plans for each weekend and introduces the friend; her mother drops the bag checks for a month. Both agreed. At the follow-up, Mrs. Iyer said, "She tells me things now. I don't need to search."

qa.q: What did Uma say she mostly does in the evenings?
qa.a: Music, and time with one friend.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Iyer feel about Uma's changes?
qa.a: Worried and shut out; she said she felt locked outside her daughter's life.

qa.q: What experiment did the counsellor suggest?
qa.a: Uma shares her weekend plans and introduces her friend, and her mother drops the bag checks for a month.

qa.q: What changed for Uma when she saw her mother's face?
qa.a: She stopped rolling her eyes, seeing that her mother was hurt rather than simply controlling.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a parent who clamped down after her teen changed and feels shut out, and how the teen's open sharing reduces the need for control.

passage:
I'm Tanvir. When I was sixteen, Abbu put a monitoring app on my phone. Every search, every chat, he could see. I felt like I was living under a CCTV camera. I deleted messages even when they were harmless, just to feel I had some privacy.
My friend Varun said, "Easy. Make a second account. They'll never know." For one night I thought about it. But I knew that if Abbu found it, I would never get his trust back.
So I asked him straight: "Why? What happened?" He told me about a boy in a colleague's family who got caught in an online scam. He was scared. I said, "Then tell me what I need to show you for this app to go." We agreed on three months, and I would tell him about new contacts myself. After three months, he deleted it in front of me.

qa.q: What did Varun suggest?
qa.a: Making a second account the parents would never know about.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel with the monitoring app?
qa.a: Uneasy and trapped, as if living under a CCTV camera, deleting even harmless messages to feel some privacy.

qa.q: Why was asking Abbu directly better than a secret account?
qa.a: It uncovered his real fear and created a clear path to trust, while a secret account could have destroyed trust if found.

qa.q: What was behind Abbu's decision?
qa.a: Fear, after a boy in a colleague's family got caught in an online scam.

grounding: A teenager whose phone is monitored feels watched, rejects a secret account and asks for a reason and a path to more trust.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday
Madhav was referred after his mother, Mrs. Ganga Rao, found a second social media account he had hidden from her. She has checked his phone every night since. Madhav said, "She reads everything. I made the other account just to breathe." His mother replied, "And now I can't believe anything you show me."
Both were hurt. I asked Madhav what he needed: a reason, and a way to earn back privacy. I asked his mother what she needed: to know who he talks to, and no more hidden accounts.
They agreed that he would delete the second account in front of her and tell her about new online contacts himself, and she would move from nightly checks to a weekly talk. We will review in six weeks. Madhav left saying, "I didn't know she was that scared."

qa.q: How often will Mrs. Rao talk with Madhav instead of checking nightly?
qa.a: Weekly.

qa.q: Why did Madhav make the second account?
qa.a: He felt watched and suffocated by the nightly checks and wanted space to breathe.

qa.q: How did the secret account backfire, and what plan rebuilt trust?
qa.a: It made his mother doubt everything; the plan was to delete it in front of her, share new contacts himself and move to weekly talks.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Rao see the hidden account?
qa.a: As broken trust; she can no longer believe what he shows her, and her checking comes from fear.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a monitored teen whose secret account damaged trust, and how a clear reason and a path to trust replace constant checking.

passage:
Sunday night
Family lunch today. Ojas got 98 in the pre-boards, and Papa said, in front of everyone, "Abhinav, be a little like Ojas, na." Everyone laughed as if it was a joke. I laughed too. Then I went up to the terrace and felt broken, like Papa would love me more if I were Ojas.
Chachi found me up there. I didn't plan to tell her, but it came out. She listened and said, "Your father's fear talks loudly. It isn't the truth about you."
She asked what I want for myself. I said 75 in maths, and to finish my robotics project. She said those are real goals and I should write them down, so I did, on my wall.
I still feel small tonight. But the list is mine, not Ojas's.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Ojas get in the pre-boards?
How did Abhinav feel on the terrace?
qa.a: Small and broken, as if Papa's love depended on Abhinav being like Ojas.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav hold on to a sense of worth?
qa.a: Telling Chachi, a trusted adult, and writing down Abhinav's own goals.

qa.q: How does Chachi see Papa's comparison?
qa.a: As his fear talking loudly, not the truth about Abhinav.

grounding: A teenager told to be like a topper cousin feels small and defective, names the hurt to a trusted adult and keeps their own goals.

passage:
In board-exam month, with every room in their small flat taken, Mummy put cousin Amandeep in Parul's room to study. "Learn from him. He gets up at five," Mummy said. It was the hundredth comparison.
Parul stopped speaking to Amandeep. She played music while he studied and let his chai go cold on purpose. Part of her even thought about skipping her own revision, just to show Mummy that comparing didn't work.
On the third night she found Amandeep asleep over his books, a sticky note on his forehead that said "Physics = doom". She almost laughed. He was just as scared as she was.
The next morning she caught Mummy alone in the kitchen. "Mummy, every time you say learn from Amandeep, I feel like I'm not enough. I'm working hard. Can you help me with my own timetable instead?"
Mummy put down the ladle. "I didn't know it hurt that much." They made the timetable that evening.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's sticky note say?
qa.a: "Physics = doom".

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she let Amandeep's chai go cold?
qa.a: Resentful of Mummy's comparisons, and taking it out on Amandeep, who had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: What did Parul do that worked better than sabotaging her revision?
qa.a: She told Mummy privately how the comparison felt and asked for help with her own timetable.

qa.q: How did Mummy react to Parul's words?
qa.a: She was surprised and said she hadn't known it hurt so much, then made the timetable with her that evening.

grounding: A teenager who resents her parent and a blameless cousin over comparisons tells the parent how it lands and asks for support with her own targets.

passage:
At Bhavna didi's engagement, the banquet hall was so loud Aadhya could barely hear herself think. Then, at the long dinner table, Mummy's voice cut through: "Bhavna got 96 in boards. Aadhya, only 74. What will we do with her?" Twelve relatives looked at her. An uncle laughed. Aadhya stared at her paneer, cheeks burning. It wasn't her fault that Mummy got nervous around her sisters, but it felt like it was.
She didn't argue in front of everyone. Later, while the band played, she found Mummy by the dessert counter. "Mummy, please don't compare my marks in front of the family. I feel judged by everyone. I'm working on maths. I went from 58 to 74. That's my progress."
Mummy blinked. "I just get nervous when my sisters start boasting." She squeezed Aadhya's hand. "From 58 to 74. I'll say that next time."

qa.q: What mark was Aadhya's compared with Bhavna's 96?
How did Aadhya feel when twelve relatives looked at her?
qa.a: Judged and ashamed; her cheeks burned.

qa.q: How did Aadhya handle it wisely?
qa.a: She did not argue in public, then privately asked Mummy to stop comparing and pointed to her own progress from 58 to 74.

qa.q: What was behind Mummy's comparison?
qa.a: Her own nerves and pride when her sisters start boasting.

grounding: A teenager compared aloud at a family gathering feels judged, sees the parent's anxiety as the source, and privately asks her to stop while showing her own progress.

passage:
Every Diwali at Nani's Mumbai flat, Papa played the same game. "Ankita has three swimming medals now. Seema, what do you have?" This year he said it while the whole family was lighting diyas on the balcony. Aunties made sympathetic noises. Ankita, holding the matchbox, looked as awkward as Seema felt.
Seema's face went hot. She thought of the sketchbook under her bed, full of drawings nobody asked about. None of this was her fault. Papa always got loud when his elder brother was around.
She waited until the next morning, when Papa was alone with his tea. "Papa, when you compare me with Ankita in front of everyone, I feel small. Please stop. I'm not a swimmer. But the school has picked three of my drawings for the art exhibition."
Papa's cup stopped halfway. "Three? Why didn't you tell me?"
"You never asked," she said quietly.
He put the cup down. "I'm asking now."

qa.q: How many swimming medals does Ankita have?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when Papa asked what she had?
qa.a: Judged and small; her face went hot in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Seema do to handle the pressure?
qa.a: She waited to speak to Papa alone, asked him to stop comparing, and shared her own achievement on her own terms.

qa.q: How did Ankita seem to feel during the comparison?
qa.a: Awkward, just like Seema, standing there holding the matchbox.

grounding: A teenager compared aloud at a family gathering feels judged, asks her parent privately to stop and shows her effort on her own terms.
